-- A bare closure used as the iterator. Each call returns the next value or -- `nil` to stop. No interface needed; the loop drives the closure directly. fn counter(stop: integer) -> fn(): integer? local i: integer = 0 return fn => () -> integer? i = i + 1 if i > stop then return nil end return i end end
class Main static fn main() for n in counter(3) do println(n) end end end

option.value:
-- A class that implements the built-in `Iterable<T>` interface. Its `iter()` -- returns a closure that yields the next value (or nil) each call. class Range implements Iterable<integer> local lo: integer local hi: integer
fn init(lo: integer, hi: integer) self.lo = lo self.hi = hi end
fn iter() -> fn(): integer? local i: integer = self.lo - 1 local stop: integer = self.hi return fn => () -> integer? i = i + 1 if i > stop then return nil end return i end end end
class Main static fn main() for n in Range(1, 4) do println(n) end end end

option.name: originalContent
option.value:
-- Multi-value iteration via `Iterable2<K, V>`. The closure returns two values -- per step (and `nil, nil` to terminate). The loop binds `name, level` -- positionally. class PlayerList implements Iterable2<string, integer> local names: table<integer, string> local levels: table<integer, integer> local count: integer
fn init() self.names = {} self.levels = {} self.count = 0 end
fn add(name: string, level: integer) self.count = self.count + 1 self.names[self.count] = name self.levels[self.count] = level end
fn iter() -> fn(): (string?, integer?) local i: integer = 0 local total: integer = self.count local ns: table<integer, string> = self.names local ls: table<integer, integer> = self.levels return fn => () -> (string?, integer?) i = i + 1 if i > total then return nil, nil end return ns[i], ls[i] end end end
class Main static fn main() local players: PlayerList = PlayerList() players:add("alice", 10) players:add("bob", 7) players:add("carol", 3)
for name, lvl in players do println(name, " -> ", lvl) end end end
